Guidance: Oversized EC2 instances chosen 'to be safe' are one of the largest sources of avoidable cloud spend; most workloads run well below the CPU/memory profile of their instance class.
Do: Right-size using CloudWatch/Compute Optimizer data after 2+ weeks of real traffic, not guesswork at launch.
Don't: Pick a large instance type at launch and never revisit it.

Keywords: s3 bucket policy, public access, data exposure, block public access
Guidance: A misconfigured S3 bucket policy or ACL can expose sensitive data to the entire internet; this remains one of the most common cloud data breach causes.
Do: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level and use bucket policies with explicit principals instead of ACLs.
Don't: Grant s3:GetObject to Principal: '*' without a CloudFront OAC in front of it.

Keywords: iam policy, least privilege, wildcard permissions, access analyzer
Guidance: Broad IAM policies using Resource: '*' and Action: '*' (or attaching AdministratorAccess to service roles) turn any single compromised credential into a full account takeover.
Do: Scope IAM policies to specific actions and resource ARNs, and use IAM Access Analyzer to find over-permissioned roles.
Don't: Attach AdministratorAccess to an application's execution role for convenience.

Keywords: lambda cold start, timeout, provisioned concurrency, vpc lambda
Guidance: Lambda functions in a VPC or with large deployment packages suffer multi-second cold starts, and a timeout set too low silently kills otherwise-successful long calls.
Do: Use provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive functions and set timeout with margin above p99 execution time, monitored via CloudWatch.
Don't: Attach every Lambda to a VPC by default and leave timeout at the 3-second default.

Keywords: vpc, subnet, public private, nat gateway, route table
Guidance: Placing databases or internal services in public subnets with public IPs unnecessarily widens the attack surface; private subnets with a NAT gateway for egress is the standard pattern.
Do: Put stateful/internal resources in private subnets and route outbound internet traffic through a NAT gateway.
Don't: Assign public IPs to RDS instances or internal app servers for convenience.

Keywords: rds backup, multi-az, point-in-time recovery, disaster recovery
Guidance: Single-AZ RDS instances have no automatic failover, and disabled automated backups mean a bad migration or accidental DROP TABLE is unrecoverable.
Do: Enable Multi-AZ for production RDS and confirm automated backups + point-in-time recovery windows meet your RPO.
Don't: Run production RDS Single-AZ with backups disabled to save cost.

Keywords: eks, node group, managed node group, karpenter, cluster autoscaler
Guidance: Static EKS node groups sized for peak load waste money at idle and under-provision during bursts; Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler with mixed instance types handles both better.
Do: Use Karpenter (or Cluster Autoscaler) with spot + on-demand mixed node pools instead of a single fixed-size managed node group.
Don't: Size a single managed node group for peak traffic and leave it static year-round.

Topic: CloudWatch alarms on the wrong signals
Keywords: cloudwatch alarm, sns, metric alarm, alerting
Guidance: Alarming only on infrastructure metrics (CPU, memory) misses user-facing failures; without alarms tied to error rates/latency and an SNS action, incidents go unnoticed until customers complain.
Do: Alarm on customer-facing SLIs (error rate, p99 latency, queue depth) in addition to infra metrics, wired to SNS/PagerDuty.
Don't: Create CloudWatch alarms with no configured action, or only alarm on CPU utilization.

Keywords: security group, 0.0.0.0/0, ingress rule, ssh exposed
Guidance: Security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH (22) or database ports are routinely found and exploited by automated internet scanners within minutes of creation.
Do: Restrict SSH/RDP/DB ports to specific known CIDRs or a bastion/SSM, never 0.0.0.0/0.
Don't: Open port 22 or 3389 to 0.0.0.0/0 'temporarily' for debugging.

Topic: Unattached EBS volumes and idle resources
Keywords: ebs volume, unattached, cost control, idle resources
Guidance: Deleted EC2 instances leave their EBS volumes and old snapshots behind by default, silently accumulating storage cost for resources nothing is using.
Do: Regularly audit for unattached EBS volumes, unused Elastic IPs, and idle load balancers via Cost Explorer or Trusted Advisor.
Don't: Terminate instances without checking for orphaned EBS volumes and Elastic IPs.

Keywords: route53, health check, dns failover, latency routing
Guidance: Without Route53 health checks tied to a failover or latency-based routing policy, DNS keeps sending traffic to a dead endpoint until a human intervenes.
Do: Attach health checks to Route53 records and use failover or latency routing policies for multi-region resilience.
Don't: Use a simple A record with no health check for a production endpoint that has a standby region.

Keywords: autoscaling group, elb health check, launch template, scaling policy
Guidance: An ASG using only EC2 status checks (not ELB health checks) will keep an instance in rotation that's failing at the application layer but still 'running' at the instance layer.
Do: Configure ASG health check type ELB so unhealthy-at-the-app-layer instances get replaced, and use a launch template (not launch config) for new ASGs.
Don't: Leave ASG health check type as EC2 for a web-facing service behind a load balancer.

Keywords: root account, mfa, access keys, break glass
Guidance: Using the AWS root account for daily work, or leaving it without MFA, means a single leaked credential compromises the entire account with no guardrails.
Do: Enable MFA on the root account, remove/never create root access keys, and use it only for the handful of tasks that require it.
Don't: Generate long-lived access keys for the root account and use them in automation.

Keywords: lambda execution role, iam, least privilege, resource policy
Guidance: The default pattern of copy-pasting a broad execution role across Lambda functions means one function's vulnerability can touch resources it never needed access to.
Do: Give each Lambda function its own execution role scoped only to the specific resources (tables, buckets, queues) it actually touches.
Don't: Share one broad execution role across every Lambda function in an account.
